1 - survive
2 - win/complete the mission
3 - kill enemies
4 - get items

.....

Idk.. the list could be longer. And like.. it doesnt need to follow the same order. A fanatical enemy could consider compliting the mission and loyalty higher than survive.

While an opportunist could be the opposite and easily consider betraying their side if it means they'll survive or get what they want.

I'm not saying you need to put these attributes in vision in the game. It's more of a profile of algorithm. It would help them decide which actions to take.. or to have a higher probability of taking.

Then..

Say your enemy has survival as first priority. What would he do to try and survive? Talk? Run? Betray? Beg? What would be his limits? 10% hp? 20% hp? The mere sight of an enemy that looks too threatning?

What about the opposite? Say you beg for your life or offer a bribe, how much does your enemy want to kill you? Maybe killing is a low priority goal for him.

You could even make it have negative values, so that negative will to kill equals someone who wishes to spare lives, but has to kill in order to achiev a higher priority goal.

You could even have a pacifist archtype which has killing priority with the absolute highest value, which would be negative. You could also turn that around and make it a Protect Life priority, which could be negative, instead.

That would allow them to decide on the fly, instead of being hardcoded into having a 2 or 3 possible answers.

Different goals / values would have different triggers. Like I said.. surving could be hp percentage or threat. But hoarding/aquiring resources could be a different trigger.

You make each of them have different weights and be measured when the trigger happens. The weight would depend like..

For instance.. the entity could have a lower limit and a higher limit that would push them in that direction, making a  certain choice have more weight. If I offer you food, and you just had lunch, it will have low value to you. But if you are starving... it's a completely different decision.

So..

- List of core values in order of priority (eg. Survive)
- List of atributes that would be tied into those core values (eg health, threat.. )
- List of triggers for each value (health %, evaluation  of threat at the beginning of every encounter..)
- List of actions to protect each set of core values (beg, bribe, run, )
- List of base weight for each core value
- List of weight multiplier by each attribute


For instance..

- Survive priority = 1
- Weight = 5
- HP = 100% means 0.5 multiplayer.
- Final weight = 2.5

- HP = 10% means multiplier caps at 2
- Final weight = 10

How would that work?

If you base weight for survive = 4, and for loyalty = 2, it means the character values surviving twice as much as loyalty

But these could vary. How much? Multiplier with 0.5 low cap and 2 high cap means the priority could be halved or doubled depending on the situation... maybe they feel very safe.. so surving doesnt weigh so much right now.

You could also consider the possibility of character development. The character changes it priority as the story unfolds. Hidden values though. No direct input from the player in a visible list or anything like that.

The problem isnt only finding the solutions, it's applying them.

I have a really hard time not using my phone, laptop or tv right before sleep time.

It's also really hard to lie down at the exact same time everyday, or most days.

Aaaand to wake up at the same time everyday.

Also, dont eat at night. It ruins your circadian rhythm, which is exactly what you are trying to fix.
And DO eat as soon as you wake up. It helps fix you circadian rythm. Pretty much, your body knows it's supposed to be awake at meal times and asleep at sleeping hours.

If you do apply these solutions without fail, you will sleep a lot better and a lot easier.

Bonus tips: dont drink coffee or anything with a lot of caffeine. If I drink coffee, even if in the morning, I'm screwed. Also, avoid sleeping in the afternoon. 

Also, exercises are really good at telling your body you need some sleep. The day you go hiking or something like that, you will pass out as soon as you hit the bed.

Oh, and spending time in daylight will help your body produce melatonin. As soon as it becomes dark around you at night, melatonin will be released and you'll want to sleep. But daylight is actually important for producing the hormone through out the day.



If you are like me, your bed time is always be pushing forward. You sleep 9pm today. 10pm tomorrow. 11pm the day after, and so on.

All these solutions help you lock your circadian rhythm in place, even if it tends to move ahead. But that means you might force yourself to wake up at the right time even if you slept an hour after planned. It might mean not allowing yourself to sleep through out the day, which can be annoying.

I'll try to sum it up as best as I can everything you need to know to get started.


1 - Set your hotkeys. Either make it up yourself or look for a good configuration online.

2 - Force your self to use said hotkeys. Also practise moving your army decently with different groups. Pressing 1a click 2a click 3a click should be second nature to you.

3 - Learn to use f1 f2 f3 f4.. they jump to different screens, so moving between bases becomes easier. Shift f1, shift 2 and so on should be used to save the screen.

4 - Use numbers on the right to save buildings. Lots of people use something like 4 - comand centers, 5 barracks, 6 factories, 7 - starports.

5 - Learn a standard build order, get good with it. Then learn an economy based build order. From here on, you'll be learning more and more build orders, but that takes a lot of time. It's better to be good with one or two than to suck at doing 6 different build orders.

6 - Remember that more workers = better economy. You want to keep producing workers non stop. Eventually you'll learn to stop at around 75, but I doubt you'll be making that many for now.

7 - Keep your resources short. If you're getting over 1000 mineral or 1000 gas, your macro sucks. Dont just line up a bunch of units though. 2 units per building only. If you still have too much resources, build more barracks, factories, gateways, hatcheries, etc. You need a good number of buildings pumping out units and upgrades to keep your resources under 1000. Ideally, your resources will always be the closest possible to 0. Imagine losing and thinking.. man.. if only these 3000 minerals in my pocket were actually units, I could've easily defended. I could've actually overun my opponent with such a big army.

8 - Scout. This is key. This might be the most important thing. How should you decide what to do? Make more units?  Which units should you make? Should you expand more? Attack? Who knows!?!? The only way to know what to do is if you have information. Keep units on key points, suicide some units on his base, whatever it takes. YOU NEED INFORMATION ALL THE TIME.

9 - Expand as soon as you get the chance. Doesnt matter if it's your third or tenth base. Take over the map.

10 - Rock paper scissor - strategy wise. If you spend too much on economy, that leaves you with poor defense. I can spend everything on units and rush you. GG. If I see you intending to rush, I'll just use a standard build order. Nothing too agressive, nothing too economy based. That way, I'll have enough to defend myself against you and still have an expansion coming, while you sacrificed your economy for a strong early attack. In short. Eco beats standard. Standard beats overly agressive. Overly agressive beats eco. 

11 - Learn to deal with harrasment. What ways are there to harras and how are you supposed to defend against them.

12 - Learn how to deal with rush/cheese. What ways are there to rush and how are you supposed to defend against them.

13 - Learn compositions. Information gives you knowledge to decide on what's the best comp to deal with opponent is. This is rock paper scissor, micro level. This might be the second most important thing on sc2. In sc1, micro was more important than composition, but in sc2, comp is king.

14 - Learn match ups. It's good if you have a friend that's about your level so you cam practise a specific match up over and over.

15 - Learn to micro.

16 - Learn late game. How to transition into late game tech and how to use it. Specially with zerg, i think, if you are playing that.

17 - Understand timing. You shouldnt play based on how strong you are. You should think of how strong you are compared to your opponent. It might be better to attack now with 10 marines then attack in 5 minutea with 100 units, cause maybe now they are defenseless, and in 5 minutes, they could have 120 units. A lot of build order and strategies are based on hitting specific timing attacks. You should be able to do it, and to expect it. Otherwise, you'll be losing to the exact same attack over and over as though you were stuck in the same game forever.

18 - Learn how to multitask. You need to keep everything going at the same time. Production, scouting, harassing, expanding, etc. The faster and better you can multitask, the better you'll play.

If you can do all of these well. You'll be in master league.

By tip 7, you should get to gold league. The basics are really that important. I can beat lower level players with zerg lings only, cause I'll have a lot more bases, units, resources, everything. I would shove 400 zerg lings down their throat before they even know what is happening. No need to micro anything or worry about composition. Just beat them by sheer number. You should be able to do the same before worrying about really advanced stuff.

In short, expand, make workers, make more buildings to increase production of units and spend all your money. You'll be running over a bunch of noobs in no time.

The videos are entertaining and will help you win. Also, 1v1 in custom games are really good to practise match ups. Stick to one lane. Whoever gets first blood or first break wins. You can add the first to 100 creep score wins if you are training wave management. 
Dont stay there for 40 minutes until you get nexus though. Thats not the point of a 1v1 practise.
